# 5 Starter Prompts for Gemini in Google Classroom (And How Students Can Use Them)

> **In short:** Google is rolling out Gemini starter prompts inside Google Classroom for students of all ages — short, guided questions that help kids use AI for studying without staring at a blank text box. Below are five concrete starter prompts students can copy, adjust, and paste right into the Gemini tab.

You've just sat down with a chapter of biology and a highlighter in your hand. The textbook is dense, the deadline is Friday, and you wish someone could just explain the hard parts in plain English. That is exactly the kind of moment Google is trying to design for with its new Gemini starter prompts inside Classroom.

## What changed (and what didn't)

Gemini is Google's AI assistant — think of it as a chat partner that can read, summarize, and explain things in plain language. Google has been adding it to Classroom over the past year, first for teachers planning lessons, then for college students 18 and older. The latest change opens it up to K-12 students (kindergarten through 12th grade) whose schools have already opted in.

The new piece is a set of **starter prompts** — pre-written questions that appear when a student opens the Gemini tab. Instead of staring at an empty box thinking *"what do I even ask?"*, students see a small menu of guided options tuned to what they're doing in class.

One important detail: a student can only use this if their **school administrator has turned it on**. If you don't see the Gemini tab in your Classroom, it's not you — it's a setting your school controls.

## Five starter prompts worth trying

Here are five prompt ideas, written so you can copy the wording, adjust it to your own assignment, and paste it into the Gemini tab. Each one is shaped around a study task students actually do.

**1. "Explain this like I'm 12."**
Great when a textbook chapter is full of jargon (specialized vocabulary you don't use in everyday speech). Paste a paragraph, then ask Gemini to rewrite it at a lower reading level. You still learn the same idea, but the words stop getting in the way.

> 💬 *Try this:* "Explain the paragraph I pasted above like I'm in 7th grade. Keep the science terms but use everyday examples."

**2. "Quiz me on this chapter."**
Turns passive reading into active recall (testing yourself instead of just rereading — one of the most effective study techniques). Paste your notes or a section of text, then ask for a short quiz. Better yet, ask for the answers *separately* so you can check yourself honestly.

> 💬 *Try this:* "Make 10 multiple-choice questions about the chapter I pasted. After I answer, give me the correct ones with a one-sentence explanation each."

**3. "What am I missing?"**
Useful after you've written a draft of an essay. Paste your draft and ask Gemini to act as a reader who is seeing it for the first time. It will often flag arguments you skipped or sentences that don't quite make sense — without rewriting your voice.

> 💬 *Try this:* "Read my essay draft below. Tell me which parts are unclear, where I jump to a conclusion without evidence, and which sentences sound repetitive."

**4. "Make a study plan from this syllabus."**
For the start of a new unit. Paste the unit outline or your notes on what's coming, and ask for a week-by-week plan. You stay in charge of the schedule — Gemini just helps you see the whole mountain before you start climbing it.

> 💬 *Try this:* "Here's our unit plan for the next three weeks. Build me a daily 30-minute study schedule leading up to the test, balancing reading, practice problems, and review."

**5. "Summarize our class discussion."**
After a busy class where you only caught half of what the teacher said. Type out the bits you remember (or paste your own notes) and ask Gemini to organize them into a clean summary, with gaps clearly marked as things you still need to ask about.

> 💬 *Try this:* "Here are my rough notes from today's history class. Organize them into a clear summary. Flag anything that looks incomplete and list questions I should ask the teacher."

## How to get the most out of it

A few habits make these prompts much more useful:

- **Be specific.** "Help me with history" is too vague. "Help me understand why the Treaty of Versailles failed" gives Gemini something to work with.
- **Paste the actual material.** The AI works much better when it has the textbook passage, your notes, or your draft in front of it, instead of working from memory.
- **Treat the answer as a starting point, not a finished one.** Gemini can confidently make things up — that's called a **hallucination** (when AI invents facts and presents them as true). Always check important facts against your textbook or teacher.
- **Use it to think, not to skip thinking.** The point is to learn the material faster — not to copy answers you don't understand.

## What this means for you

- **If you're a student:** Start with one starter prompt on something you're studying right now. Don't try all five at once — pick the one that matches your actual homework tonight.
- **If you're a parent:** Ask your child to show you the Gemini tab in Classroom. You don't need to be an AI expert — just check that they're using it to *learn* the material, not to skip it.
- **If you're a teacher:** These prompts are a starting point. You can suggest your favorites to students, or even paste a few into your assignment instructions so everyone starts from the same place.

## Wrap-up

Gemini starter prompts inside Google Classroom are basically a small menu of "good first questions" — designed so students don't have to figure out how to talk to an AI on their own. Try one prompt tonight on real homework, and notice whether the answer actually helps you understand the material better. That's the only test that matters.
